issues.legal_issue: Consent to an adoption by a statutory guardianship authority does not prevent a civil court from deciding whether the adoption is valid under personal law.
material_facts: A widow whose estate was under the charge of the Court of Wards obtained its consent before adopting a child.
A successor claimant challenged the adoption in a civil suit, alleging that the deceased husband had not authorized the widow to adopt.
The Court of Wards had considered the question of authority when deciding whether to consent to the adoption.
issues.conclusion: The civil court was competent to reconsider whether the husband had authorized the adoption; the authority's consent did not make its conclusion on that question immune from challenge.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 37 of the U.P. Court of Wards Act, 1912, consent in writing is a prerequisite to an adoption by a ward, and an adoption without it is ineffective. But consent removes only that statutory obstacle; it does not cure a defect under personal law or replace required competence, ceremonies, or observances. Section 53 bars suits to challenge or compel the authority's exercise of discretion, but does not bar a suit challenging the adoption itself. No earlier case is relied on for this holding.

rule.if: civil_suit_challenges_adoption and ward_authority_consented and (personal_law_validity_disputed or essential_adoption_requirements_disputed)

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_adoption: A civil suit was brought to challenge the validity of an adoption.
predicates.ward_authority_consented: The statutory authority responsible for the ward gave consent to the proposed adoption.
predicates.personal_law_validity_disputed: A party disputed whether the adoption complied with the personal law applicable to the person adopting.
predicates.essential_adoption_requirements_disputed: A party disputed whether the adoption satisfied essential requirements such as competence or required ceremonies.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges an adoption despite the statutory authority's consent and raises a dispute about personal-law validity or essential requirements, the civil court can decide the adoption's validity.

issues.legal_issue: Statements made during an administrative consent inquiry long after the alleged grant of authority are not admissible under the cited exceptions to prove that authority.
material_facts: The alleged authority to adopt was said to have been given many years before the statements relied on were made.
The statements were made during a later inquiry conducted to decide whether the Court of Wards should consent to an adoption.
The statements were oral, and the inquiry was not one in which an authority legally competent to determine the alleged grant of authority was investigating that fact.
issues.conclusion: The statements from the later inquiry could not be used by the civil court to prove that the husband had authorized the adoption.
issues.legal_principle: Section 157 of the Indian Evidence Act permits a former statement to corroborate testimony if it was made at or about the time of the fact, or before an authority legally competent to investigate that fact. The statements were made decades after the alleged authority and in an inquiry for consent, not before an authority competent to determine the fact. Section 32(7) concerns statements contained in deeds, wills, or other documents relating to transactions of the kind described in section 13; it does not admit oral evidence of the statements at issue. Section 32(5) was not relied on, and the statements were made after the dispute had arisen.

rule.if: adoption_authority_is_disputed and prior_statements_are_offered_to_prove_authority and statements_made_long_after_alleged_authority and statements_made_in_consent_inquiry and statements_are_oral

predicates.adoption_authority_is_disputed: A party disputes whether the person adopting had authority to do so under personal law.
predicates.prior_statements_are_offered_to_prove_au: A party offers earlier statements as evidence that the authority to adopt was given.
predicates.statements_made_long_after_alleged_autho: The statements were made long after the alleged grant of authority.
predicates.statements_made_in_consent_inquiry: The statements were made in an inquiry whose purpose was to decide whether an authority should consent to an adoption.
predicates.statements_are_oral: The statements offered are oral statements rather than statements contained in a qualifying deed, will, or other document.

issues.definition: When oral statements made long after an alleged grant of authority are offered to prove it in an adoption dispute, and they were made in a consent inquiry, those statements are not admissible for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A long delay in challenging an adoption does not by itself bar the challenge where the claimant consistently denied its validity.
material_facts: The suit challenging the adoption was filed more than fifteen years after it had occurred.
The adopted person had generally been treated as legally adopted during that period.
The claimant had earlier challenged another adoption and denied that the deceased husband had authorized his widow to adopt, and continued to deny the validity of the later adoption.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was not barred from challenging the adoption merely because the suit was brought after a long period during which others treated the adoption as valid.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the claimant was not concluded by any rule of law from questioning the adoption because he had never accepted it and had consistently denied its validity. No earlier case or statutory provision is relied on for this holding.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_adoption: A civil suit was brought to challenge the validity of an adoption.
predicates.challenge_brought_after_long_delay: The challenge was brought after a substantial period during which the adopted person was generally treated as legally adopted.
predicates.claimant_consistently_denied_adoption: The claimant had not accepted the adoption and had consistently disputed its validity.

issues.definition: A challenge brought after a long delay is not barred by delay or acquiescence when the claimant consistently denied the adoption.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily re-examine evidence for a third time when the lower courts have reached the same factual conclusion and no legal reason warrants reconsideration.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court reached the same conclusion on whether authority to adopt had been given.
The appellant asked the Supreme Court to reconsider the evidence on that factual question.
The Court found no legal reason to depart from the concurrent findings and declined to review the evidence at large.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to reconsider the evidence on the disputed factual question.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied its settled practice not to examine evidence at large, particularly where the trial court and the High Court have reached identical conclusions, absent a legal reason warranting a different conclusion. No earlier case is cited for this practice in the judgment.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and lower_courts_reached_same_factual_conclusion and appellant_seeks_reassessment_of_evidence and no_legal_reason_warrants_reassessment

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.lower_courts_reached_same_factual_conclu: The trial court and the appellate court reached the same conclusion on the disputed factual issue.
predicates.appellant_seeks_reassessment_of_evidence: The appellant asks the Supreme Court to reassess the evidence on that issue.
predicates.no_legal_reason_warrants_reassessment: The Court finds no legal reason that warrants reaching a different factual conclusion.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, when the lower courts agree on a factual conclusion and no legal reason warrants reassessment, the Court declines to reweigh the evidence.
